```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)

# fill-in table drawn as a plot; "" leaves a cell blank; fill_cols are drawn in the answer
# color, italic
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, family = "serif", fill_cols = integer(0)) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = family)
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      ans <- j %in% fill_cols
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    col = if (ans) ans_col else "black", font = if (ans) 3 else 1)
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}

library(splines)
library(mgcv)
chl <- read.csv("../../data/ReservoirChlorophyll.csv")

# Part 2: unpenalized splines
Ks <- c(4, 8, 12, 20)
fits_bs <- lapply(Ks, function(K) lm(log_chl ~ bs(week, df = K), data = chl))
aics <- sapply(fits_bs, AIC)

# Part 3: penalized spline by hand
B <- bs(chl$week, df = 20, intercept = TRUE)
pnll <- function(par, lambda) {
  beta <- par[1:20]
  -sum(dnorm(chl$log_chl, B %*% beta, exp(par[21]), log = TRUE)) +
    lambda * sum(diff(beta, differences = 2)^2)
}
check_val <- pnll(c(rep(1, 20), log(0.2)), lambda = 10)
lambdas <- c(0, 10, 1000)
fits_pen <- lapply(c(lambdas, 1e6), function(l) optim(c(rep(1, 20), log(0.2)), pnll, lambda = l,
                                                      method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 2000)))
stopifnot(all(sapply(fits_pen, `[[`, "convergence") == 0))
sig_hat <- sapply(fits_pen, function(f) exp(f$par[21]))
pen_term <- mapply(function(f, l) l * sum(diff(f$par[1:20], differences = 2)^2), fits_pen, c(lambdas, 1e6))
B_grid <- predict(B, newx = 1:52)
week_fine <- seq(1, 52, by = 0.1)
B_fine <- predict(B, newx = week_fine)
curve_pen <- sapply(fits_pen, function(f) B_fine %*% f$par[1:20])

# Part 4: mgcv
fit_gam <- gam(log_chl ~ s(week, bs = "ps", k = 20), data = chl, method = "REML")
gam_edf <- sum(fit_gam$edf) - 1
gam_sigma <- sqrt(fit_gam$sig2)
gam_fine <- predict(fit_gam, data.frame(week = week_fine))
peak_week <- week_fine[which.max(gam_fine)]
peak_level <- max(gam_fine)
fit_line <- lm(log_chl ~ week, data = chl)
huge_dev <- max(abs(curve_pen[, 4] - predict(fit_line, data.frame(week = week_fine))))

plot_chl <- function(...) {
  par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
  plot(log_chl ~ week, data = chl, pch = 19, col = "grey40", xlim = c(0, 53), ylim = c(0, 2),
       xlab = "Week of the year", ylab = expression(log[10] ~ "chlorophyll a"), ...)
}
```

**NRES 746, Week 13, Lecture 2: Spline by Hand (take-home)**

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta sans-serif type; longer answers have a bar in the margin.}

**Due Monday, Nov. 23.** Work on your own. You'll need R for Parts 2-4;
try Part 1 on paper first.

A water utility samples a reservoir every week for chlorophyll *a*, an
index of algal biomass. Ice and wind cancelled 8 of last year's 52
visits. The data are log$_{10}$ chlorophyll *a* ($\mu$g/L) by week of
the year. The utility wants to know when the spring algal bloom peaks
and how big it gets, so it can time its treatment.

```{r scatter, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3.6}
plot_chl(xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i", xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = seq(0, 52, 4))
abline(v = seq(0, 52, 4), h = seq(0, 2, 0.25), col = "grey88")
points(log_chl ~ week, data = chl, pch = 19)
lines(week_fine, gam_fine, col = ans_col, lwd = 2.5, lty = 2)
legend("topright", "sample sketch", col = ans_col, lwd = 2.5, lty = 2, bty = "n", text.col = ans_col)
```

## Part 1: Your guess (on paper)

**1a.** On the figure above, sketch the smooth seasonal curve you think
lies under the noise.

\ansbegin

Sample: low in winter (about 0.3-0.5), a sharp spring bloom peaking near
week 15-16, a drop to a summer plateau near 0.9, a small fall rise near
week 40, then a decline to winter levels.

\ansend

**1b.** From your sketch, the spring bloom peaks in week \ans{about 15-16}
at log$_{10}$ chlorophyll \ans{about 1.4-1.6}.

## Part 3: A penalized spline, by hand

Use 20 cubic B-spline basis functions, with the intercept built into
the basis:

```{r basis-code, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
library(splines)
B <- bs(chl$week, df = 20, intercept = TRUE)    # 44 x 20 model matrix
```

The model is $y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)$ with
$\mu_i = \sum_{k=1}^{20} \beta_k B_k(\text{week}_i)$ (the vector of all
$\mu_i$ is `B %*% beta`), and the penalized NLL is

$$\text{NLL}_\text{pen} = -\sum_{i=1}^{44} \log p(y_i \mid \mu_i, \sigma) +
\lambda \sum_{k=3}^{20} (\beta_k - 2\beta_{k-1} + \beta_{k-2})^2$$

**3a.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Write a function `pnll(par, lambda)` that
returns $\text{NLL}_\text{pen}$, where `par` holds the 20 weights followed
by $\log\sigma$. Check it: `pnll(c(rep(1, 20), log(0.2)), lambda = 10)`
should return `r sprintf("%.2f", check_val)`.

Your value: \ans{`r sprintf("%.2f", check_val)`}

\ansbegin

```{r pnll-code, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, highlight=FALSE}
pnll <- function(par, lambda) {
  beta <- par[1:20]
  -sum(dnorm(chl$log_chl, B %*% beta, exp(par[21]), log = TRUE)) +
    lambda * sum(diff(beta, differences = 2)^2)
}
```

\ansend

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

**3b.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Minimize `pnll()` with `optim()` for each
$\lambda$ below, starting from `c(rep(1, 20), log(0.2))`. Use
`method = "BFGS"` and `control = list(maxit = 2000)`, and check
`$convergence`. Record $\hat\sigma$ and the penalty term
$\lambda \sum (\beta_k - 2\beta_{k-1} + \beta_{k-2})^2$ at the optimum.

```{r lambda-table, fig.height=2}
blank_table(
  headers = list(expression(lambda), expression(hat(sigma)), "penalty term at the optimum"),
  body = lapply(1:3, function(i) list(format(lambdas[i]), sprintf("%.3f", sig_hat[i]),
                                      sprintf("%.2f", pen_term[i]))),
  col_widths = c(1, 1.4, 2.6), fill_cols = 2:3)
```

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

**3c.** *(AI optional/encouraged.)* Plot the data with your three fitted curves
(`B_grid <- predict(B, newx = 1:52)` gives the basis at every week).
Name it **Figure 3c**.

```{r fig-3c, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3.4}
plot_chl()
for (i in 1:3) lines(week_fine, curve_pen[, i], col = ans_col, lwd = 2, lty = c(3, 1, 2)[i])
legend("topright", paste("lambda =", lambdas), col = ans_col, lwd = 2, lty = c(3, 1, 2),
       bty = "n", text.col = ans_col)
```

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

**3d.** Which $\lambda$ would you use? Why does $\hat\sigma$ change the
way it does as $\lambda$ grows?

\ansbegin

$\lambda = 10$: it follows the spring bloom without chasing single
weeks ($\lambda = 0$ wiggles; $\lambda = 1000$ flattens the bloom).
$\hat\sigma$ grows with $\lambda$ because a stiffer curve passes farther
from the points, so more of the variation is left as residual noise.

\ansend

## Part 4: The same model in mgcv

**4a.** *(AI optional/encouraged.)* Fit
`gam(log_chl ~ s(week, bs = "ps", k = 20), data = chl, method = "REML")`
(package `mgcv`), which uses the same kind of basis and penalty and
chooses $\lambda$ itself. Plot its curve with your chosen fit from 3d.
Name it **Figure 4a**.

```{r fig-4a, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3.4}
plot_chl()
lines(week_fine, curve_pen[, 2], col = ans_col, lwd = 2)
lines(week_fine, gam_fine, col = ans_col, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("pnll(), lambda = 10", "gam(), REML"), col = ans_col, lwd = 2, lty = 1:2,
       bty = "n", text.col = ans_col)
```

Effective degrees of freedom (edf): \ans{`r sprintf("%.1f", gam_edf)`} $\qquad \hat\sigma$: \ans{`r sprintf("%.3f", gam_sigma)`}

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

**4b.** When does the spring bloom peak, and at what level? Compare the

`gam()` peak: week \ans{`r sprintf("%.1f", peak_week)`} at log$_{10}$ chlorophyll \ans{`r sprintf("%.2f", peak_level)`}

\ansbegin

Sample: about where I put it, but lower than the highest single week

\ansend

**Bonus (optional).** Refit your penalized spline with
$\lambda = 10^6$ and compare its curve with `lm(log_chl ~ week, data = chl)`.
Why does a huge $\lambda$ give this curve?

\ansbegin

It is the `lm()` line to within `r sprintf("%.3f", huge_dev)` (intercept
`r sprintf("%.3f", coef(fit_line)[1])`, slope
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(fit_line)[2])` per week; nearly flat here). A
huge $\lambda$ forces every second difference of the weights to 0, so
the weights fall on a line in $k$, which makes the curve close to a
straight line (exactly straight with evenly spaced knots; `bs()` piles
up knots at the ends, which bends it slightly there). The penalty
doesn't touch a weight sequence that is itself a line, so its intercept
and slope are fit by least squares.

\ansend
